passage:
The food festival was so loud that Nazia had to shout to be heard, and the stalls were packed shoulder to shoulder. Bidisha's ice cream was melting down her wrist while Nazia held the phone up for the twelfth selfie.

"Hold on, the light's better by the lanterns," Nazia said. She posted one with the caption "Us ❤️" and refreshed to see the likes. Then she scrolled to another couple's photos: matching outfits, a sunset, hundreds of hearts. Her own picture suddenly looked plain.

She glanced up. Bidisha was standing quietly, licking her wrist clean, a little glassy-eyed with the crowd noise. They hadn't really talked in an hour.

Nazia put the phone in her pocket. "Sorry. Want to find somewhere quieter and just eat?"

Bidisha's face lit up. "Yes, please."

qa.q: How many selfies had Nazia taken when Bidisha's ice cream was melting?
qa.a: She was taking the twelfth selfie.

qa.q: What was Nazia feeling when she scrolled to the other couple's photos?
qa.a: Nazia felt insecure, as her own picture suddenly looked plain beside another couple's posts, as if she were measuring their relationship against theirs.

qa.q: What might Nazia try next time to notice whether posting is bringing them closer?
qa.a: Ask herself whether they have actually talked or enjoyed the moment together, and put the phone away when the answer is no.

qa.q: How might Bidisha have felt while Nazia kept taking photos?
qa.a: She may have felt overlooked and a bit worn out by the noise, which would explain her quiet look and her relief at the offer to go somewhere quieter.

grounding: Shows wanting the relationship seen and validated online, comparing with filtered posts, then noticing the posting had replaced time together.

subtype: Partner × Public display and social media [Actor]
passage: College counsellor's note, Thursday. Rekha (second year, commerce) came in upset after a fight with her boyfriend, Akash. She said he refused to post an anniversary photo, and she felt he was 'hiding' her. When I asked what posting meant to her, she scrolled through the couple accounts she follows: matching outfits, surprise videos, captions of eternal love. She admitted she'd been comparing their relationship with these every night and feeling it came up short. We looked at her own last month instead: long phone calls when her grandmother was ill, Akash waiting outside her exam hall, cooking together at his aunt's. She went quiet, then said, 'The good stuff wasn't online at all.' She decided to talk to Akash about why the photo had mattered to her, and to mute the couple accounts for a while. Follow-up in two weeks.

qa.q: Why did Rekha fight with Akash?
qa.a: He refused to post an anniversary photo.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel after comparing her relationship with couple accounts?
qa.a: She felt insecure and let down, as if their relationship came up short.

qa.q: What did Rekha decide after the session?
qa.a: To talk to Akash about why the photo mattered and to mute the couple accounts for a while.

qa.q: How might Akash see the anniversary photo fight?
qa.a: He may feel accused of hiding Rekha when he values private moments like waiting outside her exam hall.

grounding: A counsellor's note on a young woman wanting her relationship validated online, noticing that posts were replacing rather than reflecting closeness.

subtype: Partner × Public display and social media [Actor]
passage:
Sunday night. Today Jaya and I went to the lake for our one-year anniversary. I spent the first hour setting up photos: the right light, the boat, the matching coffee cups. I made her redo a 'candid' laugh four times. Then I posted it and kept refreshing to see who liked it. At some point I looked up and Jaya was just sitting on the bench, watching the ducks, a bit quiet. I asked if she was okay. She said, 'I miss you. You've been here all day but not really.' That hit hard. I'd been performing us instead of being with her. I scrolled back through my posts and saw that every single one was from a moment I don't really remember. I put the phone in my bag. We fed the ducks, talked about her new job, shared some terrible samosas. No photos. It was the best part of the day.
- Ishita

qa.q: How many times did Ishita make Jaya redo the 'candid' laugh?
What did Ishita feel when Jaya said 'I miss you'?
qa.a: Ishita felt a hard jolt of guilt, realising the day had gone on performing instead of being together.

qa.q: What did Ishita do to change the rest of the day?
qa.a: Put the phone away and simply fed the ducks, talked and shared samosas with Jaya, with no photos 🙂

qa.q: How was the day for Jaya before the phone went away?
qa.a: Lonely, with Ishita there all day but not really present.

grounding: A diary of a young person who notices anniversary posts replacing closeness, and puts the phone away to be present.
